blocks.text: As soon as she came there, she yoked bridled snakes to her chariot, and wanders dry-shod over the waters of the sea. [III, 232] So Ovid in book 4 of the Fasti. And Circe is carried in a chariot of dragons from Colchis to the promontory of Circeii in Italy; Medea, after killing her children, from Corinth to Athens; Triptolemus from Athens to Patrae, a coastal city of Achaea, where Antheas, the son of Eumelus, having dared after the example of Triptolemus to yoke dragons, was thrown from the chariot and perished; that is, he suffered shipwreck when, unskilled in navigation, he had ventured upon the sea. The story is found in the Achaica of Pausanias. But we argue in vain, since it is the part of a Coroebus or a Margites (that is, of fools) to believe Τριπτόλεμον ἐλάσαι διὰ τοῦ ἀέρος ἐπὶ δρακόντων ὑποπτέρων [Triptolemon elasai dia tou aeros epi drakontōn hypopterōn], that Triptolemus was carried through the air by winged dragons, as Lucian rightly asserts in the Philopseudes, mocking these fictions of the poets. In the same spirit Augustine too, or whoever is the author of the book, in book 2 of the Soliloquies, chapter 15: For when it is said that Medea flew with winged snakes yoked together, that thing in no respect imitates the truth; for it does not exist, and a thing that does not exist at all cannot imitate anything. Yet the wings of dragons arose from nowhere else than from fictions of this kind.

But there is no lack of other marks by which dragons are distinguished from the common run of serpents. Among these let the first be their vast bulk, as frequent in dragons as it is rare and unusual in the other serpents. The second, a beard and dewlaps under the chin. Nicander,
— — — νέρθε δὲ πώγων Ἔπλεθ' ὑπ' ἀνθερεῶνα χολοίβαφος, [— — — nerthe de pōgōn Epleth' hyp' anthereōna choloibaphos,]

But below, under the chin, is a yellow beard. Aelian, book 11, chapter 26: Ἔχει γοῦν ὁ μὲν δράκων ὁ ἄῤῥην τὸν λόφον, καὶ τὴν ὑπήνην δασεῖαν· [Echei goun ho men drakōn ho arrhēn ton lophon, kai tēn hypēnēn daseian;] The male dragon indeed has a crest and a shaggy beard. Avicenna: وتحت الفك الاسفل نتو كالذقن [wa-taḥt al-fakk al-asfal nutūʾ ka-l-dhaqan] And under the lower jaw (they have) a protuberance like a beard. Philostratus does not attribute a beard to all, but to a certain kind of dragons: Οἵδε δὴ πυρσῖται, he says, καὶ περιόνωτοι γίνονται, οὗτοι καὶ γενειάσκουσι· [Hoide dē pyrsitai … kai perionōtoi ginontai, houtoi kai geneiaskousi;] Those that have a fiery colour and a serrated back also grow a beard. The third, a triple row of teeth, if indeed Nicander is right,
— — — ἐν δὲ γενείῳ Τρίστιχοι ἑκάτερθε περιστιχόωσιν ὀδόντες, [— — — en de geneiō tristichoi hekaterthe peristichoōsin odontes,]

And in the jaw three rows of teeth are arranged on each side. Avicenna has only وفي كل لحي ثلثة انياب [wa-fī kull laḥy thalātha anyāb] And in each jaw there are three teeth. But I think something has been omitted, for example the word صفوف [ṣufūf] or سطور [suṭūr], that is, rows. Let the fourth mark be colour, which is indeed varied. For Aëtius observes that some are black, some reddish, some ash-coloured. And, according to Avicenna, [III, 233] لها وجوه صغر وسود [lahā wujūh ṣughr wa-sūd] Their faces are yellow and black. And long before, Nicander,
Φράζεο καὶ χλοάοντα δαεὶς κύανόν τε δράκοντα, [Phrazeo kai chloaonta daeis kyanon te drakonta,]
Being skilled, describe also the yellow and the black dragon. Yet for the most part they are described as tawny, or yellow, or golden, or reddish in colour, which is nearly the same thing. Lucan,
You dragons crawl, shining with golden gleam.

Pausanias in the Corinthiaca: Δράκοντες δὲ οἱ λοιποὶ, καὶ ἕτερον γένος, ἐς τὸ ξανθότερον ῥέποντες χρόας, ἱεροὶ μὲν τοῦ Ἀσκληπιοῦ νομίζονται· [Drakontes de hoi loipoi, kai heteron genos, es to xanthoteron rhepontes chroas, hieroi men tou Asklēpiou nomizontai;] The other [col. 436] dragons too, but (especially) another kind, inclining to a tawny colour, are held sacred to Aesculapius. And Philostratus, in the place cited above, after saying that πυρσίτας [pyrsitas] dragons (that is, of fiery colour) have a serrated back and a beard, adds: καὶ τὸν αὐχένα ὑψοῦ αἴρουσι, καὶ τὴν φολίδα στίλβουσι δίκην ἀργύρου [kai ton auchena hypsou airousi, kai tēn pholida stilbousi dikēn argyrou], and they raise their neck higher, and their scales shine like silver: so as to show that these stand out most among dragons. So that the supreme Poet did not write in vain, Iliad β΄ [b], line 308:
Ἔνθ᾽ ἐφάνη μέγα σῆμα, δράκων ἐπὶ νῶτα δαφοινός· [Enth' ephanē mega sēma, drakōn epi nōta daphoinos;]

There appeared a great sign, a dragon red on its back (or reddish). And not very differently the divine writer, Apoc. XII, 1. 3. A great sign appeared in heaven, etc. And behold a great red dragon! Although something else is signified: namely the devil, who is bloodthirsty and a murderer from the beginning, Ioh. VIII, 44, and inflamed with wrath, and burning, because his time is short, Apoc. XII, 12. With this in view the Syriac translator renders ܬܢܝܢܐ ܕܢܘܪܐ, a fiery dragon. And the Arabic: تنين بلون النار [tinnīn bi-lawn al-nār] a dragon of fiery colour. Which for Philostratus is πυρσίτης [pyrsitēs], and for John πυῤῥὸς [pyrrhos], that is, πυρόεις τὴν χροιάν [pyroeis tēn chroian].
